clue.text: Type, possibly, aiming to avoid this muscular problem?

definitions.text: Type, possibly, aiming to avoid this muscular problem?

parts.words: Type, possibly, aiming to avoid this muscular problem?
parts.note: someone who types instead of using a pen may be dodging the hand ache that comes from long hours of penmanship

explanation.surface: A question about whether choosing a typeface is a way of dodging some muscular ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' looks like a noun (a kind or a font) but is the verb: typing rather than handwriting spares the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the familiar name for a painful spasm of the hand muscles brought on by too much handwriting.

clue.text: Aspiring club worker? Sounds like it

indicators.note: the clue asks the solver to say the club-and-worker phrase out loud and hear another word

parts.note: a wood is a golf club and a bee is a worker insect, giving WOOD BEE

explanation.surface: Someone hoping to join a club as a staff member is asked whether it sounds right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'club worker' reads as someone employed at a club; it is a golf wood plus a worker bee.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspiring person hopes to become something, which is exactly the hyphenated adjective's sense.

clue.text: Man, possibly, taking time to make fibre

indicators.note: the island takes in, or holds, the time letter inside itself

parts.note: the Isle of Man is one example of an isle

explanation.surface: A man spends time weaving some sort of fibre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a person but is the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea, hinting ISLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Istle is a tough plant fibre from Mexican agave and yucca, used for cord and brushes.

clue.text: Hear piano differently with one's audio equipment

indicators.note: the letters are arranged in a different way to form a new word

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly
taken as written, the apostrophe giving no letter

explanation.surface: Someone hears a piano in a new way through their own sound kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'differently' shuffles HEAR and P into EARPH; the apostrophe in 'one's' adds no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Headphones worn over the ears are a piece of personal sound gear.

clue.text: Naturally starts to represent this element

definitions.text: Naturally starts to represent this element

parts.words: Naturally starts to represent this element
parts.note: the opening two letters of the word Naturally, Na, are the chemical symbol of the metal meant

explanation.surface: Beginnings, by nature, stand for some chemical element.
explanation.walkthrough: Na comes from the Latin natrium and is the symbol of this soft alkali metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Its chemical symbol is Na, taken from the Latin natrium, matching the first two letters of 'Naturally'.

clue.text: Remaining up to praise one's monarch

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the pieces are read from the bottom upwards, so backwards

parts.note: to laud is to praise
one is I, and 's stands for is, giving IS
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword monarch

explanation.surface: Someone stays on in order to praise their own king or queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns the whole run LAUDISER backwards in this down clue. ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, Queen Elizabeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Something residual is left over, still remaining after the rest has gone.

clue.text: Athlete Tulliver, for one, found half-hearted

indicators.note: losing half of its heart means one of the two central matching letters is dropped

parts.note: Mr Tulliver in George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss runs a mill, so he is a miller

explanation.surface: An athlete called Tulliver is found to lack commitment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-hearted' removes one of the two Ls at the heart of MILLER. Tulliver looks like an athlete's surname but is Eliot's mill owner.
explanation.definitionFit: A miler is a runner who specialises in races over one mile.

clue.text: German woman outside university has misplaced a fur

indicators.note: the anagrammed letters sit outside, around, the university letter
the letters are put in the wrong places, rearranged

explanation.surface: A German lady outside a college has lost her fur coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts the word 'has' around U; 'misplaced' rearranges A FUR into FRAU, German for woman, so the answer half-defines itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Hausfrau is German for housewife, a woman running the home.

clue.text: State's founder concerned with flag

parts.note: William Penn founded Pennsylvania, the US state named after his family
on means about or concerning

explanation.surface: The man who founded a state was worried about its banner.
explanation.definitionFit: A pennon is a long narrow pennant, a kind of banner flown from a lance or mast.

clue.text: Marge's rival losing lead, say

indicators.note: the first letter, the lead, of the word is dropped

parts.note: marge is margarine, and butter is its rival spread

explanation.surface: Marge's rival loses her lead, as you might say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marge' looks like a woman's name but is short for margarine.
explanation.definitionFit: To utter is to speak or voice words, a synonym of the verb to say.

clue.text: Offend, complaint being out of place

indicators.note: the illness word stands outside the place abbreviation, wrapping it

parts.note: a complaint can be an illness or disease
PL is a common abbreviation for place in addresses

explanation.surface: Someone causes offence by moaning when it is inappropriate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complaint' looks like a grumble but is the medical sense, an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: To displease someone is to annoy or upset them, as offending does.

clue.text: Canon seen by river consuming hot dog

indicators.note: the canon piece comes after, seen beside, the river

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland

indicators.note: the round eats, holds inside, the letter for hot

parts.note: a canon in music is a round, voices entering in turn
H is the abbreviation for hot on taps

explanation.surface: A clergyman spotted by a riverbank eating a hot dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canon' suggests a cleric, but it is a musical round; H goes inside ROUND after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A deerhound is a large rough-coated Scottish hunting breed, a dog.

clue.text: Quit, having removed good stuff from trunk

indicators.note: the letter for good is taken out of the word for quit

parts.note: to quit a job is to resign

explanation.surface: Someone stops work after clearing good items out of a car boot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trunk' is not a car's boot or luggage but a tree trunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Resin is the sticky sap that oozes from the trunks of pines and other trees.

clue.text: They go off in the direction of the theatre

definitions.text: They go off in the direction of the theatre

parts.words: They go off in the direction of the theatre
parts.note: a stage direction in a play script telling the actors to leave, read as if it meant heading towards a playhouse

explanation.surface: People leaving and heading for the playhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the direction of' suggests travelling towards the theatre, but means 'as a stage direction'.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for 'they go out', this word is printed in scripts to send several actors offstage.

clue.text: Clearly show a couple of keys in this sign

indicators.note: the two keys go in the middle of the word for clearly show

parts.note: to evince is to show clearly
D and E are two musical keys

explanation.surface: A sign that clearly shows two keys inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clearly show' looks like part of the definition but is wordplay; D and E are named musical keys.
explanation.definitionFit: Evidence is a sign or indication that points to the truth of something.

clue.text: Language of a bureaucrat

definitions.meaning: the standard form of Chinese spoken in Beijing
a senior civil servant, after officials in imperial China

explanation.surface: The jargon used by a government official.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the chief Chinese tongue and a powerful, often pompous, government official.

clue.text: Bond appears extremely bizarre in false teeth

indicators.note: the extreme letters are placed inside the false teeth

parts.note: a denture is a set of false teeth

indicators.note: only the outermost letters, first and last, of the word are used

explanation.surface: A bond looks very strange when found among someone's false teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' suggests 007 or a tie, but it is a financial bond; 'extremely' picks B and E from 'bizarre'.
explanation.definitionFit: A debenture is a long-term loan certificate, a kind of bond issued by a company.

clue.text: Sticking together in business, a fellow's upset no one

parts.note: CO is short for company, a business
a fellow is he, and 's stands for is, giving HE'S

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: In a company, a man is distressed that nobody is there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns NO and I backwards to ION. 'a fellow's' is HE IS, not a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Cohesion is the act or state of holding firmly together as one unit.

clue.text: Panelling supplied with home within Berkshire town

indicators.note: the home letters go inside the name of the town

parts.note: Ascot is a town in Berkshire, England, famous for its racecourse
in means at home

explanation.surface: Wooden panelling provided for a house in an English county town.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is a Berkshire town famous for its racecourse; 'home' as IN means at home.
explanation.definitionFit: A wainscot is wooden panelling lining the lower part of a room's walls.

clue.text: Trendy comedian introducing popular success

parts.note: a wit is a clever, funny person
a hit is a popular success

explanation.surface: A fashionable comedian brings in a hit show.
explanation.definitionFit: With-it is dated slang for fashionable and up to date.

clue.text: Too big to be right, stupid

definitions.meaning: in geometry, an angle greater than ninety degrees, too large to be a right angle

explanation.surface: Someone too large to be correct is called dim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right' seems to mean correct but means a right angle.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes an angle wider than ninety degrees and also a dim, slow-witted person.

clue.text: Blow up General Assembly

indicators.note: assembly means putting parts together, here building a new word from the letters

explanation.surface: Explosion at the General Assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General Assembly' looks like the United Nations body; 'Assembly' rearranges GENERAL.
explanation.definitionFit: To blow up a photograph is to make it bigger.

clue.text: Meeting manager, half of them produce an outstanding effect

indicators.note: the second half of the word is taken, two of its four letters

parts.note: a boss is a manager

explanation.surface: At a meeting, the manager and half the staff make an outstanding impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half of' takes the back half of 'them'; 'Meeting' just says the two pieces meet side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To emboss is to raise a design so it stands out from a surface.

clue.text: In combat he tackled the leader of Thebes

indicators.note: the answer sits in the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: In battle, he took on the ruler of the Greek city of Thebes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the leader of Thebes' looks like a king; it is the Greek letter that begins Thebes in Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: Thebes is spelt in Greek with theta as its first letter, so that letter leads the name.

clue.text: Judge thrown by specialised terminology for gaseous element

indicators.note: the judge is thrown off, removed from, the word for jargon

parts.note: jargon is the specialised language of a trade or group

explanation.surface: A judge is baffled by technical talk about a gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thrown' looks like confused, but J is thrown off JARGON. The OCR added a stray apostrophe after 'terminology'.
explanation.definitionFit: Argon is an inert noble gas, chemical element number 18.

clue.text: About noon, worker lakes nearly half the cheese

indicators.note: the worker goes around, about, the noon letter

parts.note: emmet is a dialect word for an ant, the classic worker

indicators.note: nearly means almost all, so the last letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Around midday, a worker eats almost half the cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' wraps the ant around the noon letter, and 'nearly' drops the last letter of 'half'. Emmet is an old dialect word for an ant.
explanation.definitionFit: Emmenthal is a Swiss cheese with large holes, named after the Emme valley.

clue.text: Established custom associated with riding

definitions.meaning: a riding ... is the outfit worn on horseback

explanation.surface: A long-standing tradition linked to horse riding.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a settled routine and, in 'riding habit', the clothes worn on horseback.

clue.text: Popular clubs the eccentric go into in disguise

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, signalling the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Popular nightclubs are where the oddball goes when he wants to be unrecognised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' looks like a person but rearranges GO INTO to OGNITO.
explanation.definitionFit: Going incognito means hiding one's identity, so being disguised.

clue.text: Natural brown line initially removed from wood

indicators.note: the line letter is taken off the start of the wood word

parts.note: lumber is sawn timber, wood

explanation.surface: A natural brown line is removed from some wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Umber is a natural earth pigment giving a dark yellowish brown.

clue.text: Roused to best effort, regularly taking personal gold or silver, say?

parts.note: someone on a drug takes it regularly
one's means belonging to oneself, personal

indicators.note: say means the word is spoken, heard as a different spelling

parts.note: gold and silver are examples of metal

explanation.surface: Someone goes all out, routinely taking their own gold or silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gold or silver' looks like medals for effort, but means METAL, which sounds like METTLE, courage.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means spurred to do one's utmost, with courage and spirit fully aroused.
